records.content: Research news 01 Oct, 2026 Researchers have developed a rapid approach to validate diagnostic tests for Bundibugyo virus and found evidence that an existing Zaire ebolavirus vaccine could provide cross-protection, offering potential tools to strengthen responses to the 2026 outbreak The current outbreak of Bundibugyo virus (BDBV) in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has highlighted the difficulties that health authorities face when a rare and dangerous pathogen emerges for which dedicated diagnostic tests, vaccines and treatments are unavailable or at best limited. Two studies led by researchers from the German Center for Infection Research (DZIF) at Charité – Universitätsmedizin Berlin and the German Primate Center – Leibniz Institute for Primate Research in Göttingen – including international collaborators – have examined different aspects of the response. The research assessed how diagnostic tests could be evaluated rapidly and whether an established Ebola vaccine might offer some protection against BDBV. During the COVID-19 pandemic, researchers at Charité led by Professor Christian Drosten, a DZIF scientist, rapidly developed a polymerase chain reaction (PCR) assay for Sars-CoV-2 virus. Its validated design was made publicly available which allowed manufacturers and laboratories to reproduce it and helped to expand testing capacity. European Union legislation has since introduced more stringent requirements for diagnostic devices. Although intended to ensure test performance, these requirements can present difficulties during outbreaks when validated diagnostics are required rapidly and appropriate reference materials are scarce. The 2026 BDBV outbreak provided an opportunity to address this problem. BDBV belongs to the Ebolavirus genus and can cause severe Ebola virus disease but there is no vaccine or therapeutic treatment specifically licensed against it. On 20 May 2026, the Charité hospital admitted a patient from the USA who had contracted BDBV in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Researchers obtained viral genetic material from a throat swab and established a reference standard against which candidate diagnostic assays could be evaluated. The team assembled an international network of nine laboratories that included DZIF members, the German National University Medicine Network (NUM), European research consortia, university hospitals and biosafety level four laboratories – the highest laboratory containment level. The network assessed four candidate PCR tests from two manufacturers. Within two weeks, the laboratories completed analytical and clinical evaluations, with no evidence of cross-reactivity. The results demonstrated that a decentralised network could rapidly generate robust test-performance data to support regulatory assessment and deployment during an infectious disease emergency. The researchers also highlighted the importance of collaboration between publicly funded laboratories and diagnostic manufacturers. Rare pathogens provide relatively little commercial incentive to develop tests that might be required only occasionally, so public investment would be required to maintain preparedness for high-consequence diseases. A second study, led by DZIF scientist Professor Stefan Pöhlmann at the German Primate Center, examined the biological characteristics of the 2026 BDBV strain and whether vaccination against Zaire ebolavirus might offer cross-protection. Researchers focused on the viral glycoprotein, a surface protein that allows ebolaviruses to enter host cells and represents an important target for neutralising antibodies. Because authentic BDBV requires biosafety level four containment, they used pseudovirus particles that carried glycoproteins from BDBV strains associated with outbreaks in 2007–08, 2012 and 2026. The experiments found no evidence that the 2026 glycoprotein allowed more efficient entry into human cells than those from earlier strains. Researchers also examined serum from ten healthy volunteers who had received the licensed recombinant vesicular stomatitis virus-Zaire ebolavirus vaccine, known as rVSV-ZEBOV. Samples were assessed before vaccination and at 28 and 180 days afterwards. After vaccination, antibodies could neutralise pseudoviruses that carried glycoproteins from all three BDBV strains. BDBV-specific neutralising activity was detected in six of the ten vaccine recipients at both post-vaccination time points, although activity was approximately 3.5 to 3.6 times lower than against Zaire ebolavirus. The results provide evidence that antibodies elicited by the licensed vaccine can recognise and inhibit BDBV in laboratory models. However, the researchers cautioned that the experiments did not demonstrate protection against BDBV infection or disease in people because the study used pseudoviruses and measured neutralisation in vitro. Taken together, the studies demonstrate how diagnostic science, virology and immunology can provide complementary tools during an infectious disease outbreak. International laboratory networks, accessible reference materials and regulatory mechanisms established before an emergency could help to reduce the interval between identification of an emerging pathogen and access to reliable diagnostics and potential preventive measures. records.content: Health Cabinet Secretary Aden Duale said the Ministry had identified 28 contacts. Officials are also tracing 23 passengers and four crew on Jambojet flight 8523. The groups reflect different checks: exposure at home or during care, and people who shared the journey. Authorities have not said how many have completed follow-up. The Ministry said the patient, who had lived in the DRC for seven years, fell ill about a month before returning. After treatment at several DRC facilities, he travelled by road to Kampala and flew to Nairobi on 3 October. He underwent routine screening at Jomo Kenyatta International Airport, then was taken to Nairobi Hospital and isolated. Public accounts do not specify whether symptoms were evident at the airport, a detail needed to assess screening and referral without assuming a lapse. He later died despite supportive care. Authorities have not named him. Officials say 28 close contacts, including relatives and health workers, have been identified. Separately, authorities are tracing 23 passengers and four crew from the flight to Nairobi. These are response groups, not a count of infected people. The test is whether people at meaningful exposure risk can be located and monitored through the virus’s incubation period. Kenya’s first confirmed imported Ebola case has turned months of preparedness into a test of contact tracing and hospital infection control. The patient, a Kenyan returning from the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), died late on 5 October after testing positive for Bundibugyo virus disease, the Health Ministry announced the next day. Porini Point is a large, phased apartment development planned within Tatu City, a 5,000-acre mixed-use city in Kiambu County. The development is designed as a low-rise residential community containing approximately 570 apartments across 24 ground-plus-four-storey blocks. The project offers one-, two- and three-bedroom apartments arranged around landscaped courtyards and shared recreational areas. Planned amenities include a residents’ clubhouse, swimming pool and sun deck, indoor and outdoor fitness facilities, barbecue area, children’s playground, landscaped gardens, resident and visitor parking, controlled access and security services. Porini Point is positioned close to Tatu City’s schools, offices, industrial and commercial districts, healthcare services, shops, restaurants and recreation facilities. The development is also marketed for its proximity to the planned 160-acre Tatu Wildlife Sanctuary. Apartments are sold unfurnished. Published specifications include SPC parquet-style flooring in living and bedroom areas, ceramic tiles in wet areas, quartz kitchen countertops, fitted cabinetry, open-plan kitchens, hob, oven, extractor hood, laundry areas, large windows and private balconies on upper-floor units. Selected ground-floor apartments may include private gardens. The official project information states that the first three buildings are targeted for handover in Q1 2027, while the complete development is targeted for Q4 2029. Buyers should obtain a unit-specific completion date and contractual long-stop date before committing funds. One-bedroom apartment — 54 m2 The one-bedroom apartment is designed for individuals, couples, corporate tenants and investors seeking a relatively accessible entry point into Tatu City. The published layout includes: Living and dining area. Open-plan fitted kitchen. Separate bedroom. Full bathroom. Laundry area. Private balcony on upper floors. One parking space. Best suited to: young professionals, returning diaspora, corporate tenants, first-time buyers and furnished-rental investors. Two-bedroom apartment — 90 m2 Two alternative two-bedroom layouts are offered. Both include a main bedroom with an ensuite bathroom, a second bedroom, separate shared bathroom, living and dining space, fitted kitchen, laundry area and balcony. Best suited to: couples, small families, professional house-sharers and medium- to long-term tenants. Three-bedroom apartment — 145 m2 The three-bedroom configuration offers larger living accommodation, three bathrooms, a walk-in wardrobe, laundry space and two balconies. Two parking spaces are included in the published price. Best suited to: families, owner-occupiers, senior professionals and buyers prioritising space over maximum rental yield. 7. Location breakdown Where is Porini Point located? Porini Point is located inside Tatu City, near Ruiru in Kiambu County, north of Nairobi. Tatu City is accessible through several regional road connections, including Thika Superhighway, the Eastern and Northern bypasses, Kiambu Road and Ruiru–Kiambu Road. The official project material estimates approximately: 30–35 minutes to Nairobi CBD under favourable conditions. 30–32 minutes to Westlands. Approximately 30 minutes to the United Nations area. 35–45 minutes to Jomo Kenyatta International Airport. Actual travel times vary significantly with traffic and the chosen route. Nearby schools Crawford International School. Nova Pioneer Primary School. Nova Pioneer High School. Planned and developing education facilities within Tatu City. Shopping, food and services Naivas supermarket. Cafés and restaurants within Tatu City. Banking facilities. Pharmacy and healthcare services. Safaricom and everyday retail services. Tatu City commercial and office districts. Employment and business districts Tatu Industrial Park. Tatu City Special Economic Zone. Tatu Central business district. Office and co-working facilities. More than 100 operating businesses across the wider city. Recreation and green spaces Tatu City walking and cycling trails. Parks and landscaped areas. Sports and outdoor fitness facilities. Planned Tatu Wildlife Sanctuary. Porini Point clubhouse, swimming pool and play areas. The wildlife sanctuary should be described as planned or under development, not as an already operational attraction. 8. Investment section Is Porini Point a good investment? Porini Point may appeal to investors seeking exposure to a master-planned development with schools, businesses, infrastructure and residential demand in one location. Its one-bedroom apartments offer the lowest entry price and potentially the broadest tenant pool, while larger units may attract families and long-term occupants. The developer’s published model estimates monthly rents of: Unit Unfurnished estimate Furnished estimate One bedroom KES 55,000 KES 95,000 Two bedroom KES 70,000 KES 130,000 Three bedroom KES 100,000 KES 160,000 These estimates generate advertised gross yields of approximately 7%–16% against the published cash prices. They are projections rather than guaranteed returns and exclude vacancy, tax, management fees, service charges, furnishing, maintenance and transaction costs. The 21-day period is the outer edge of WHO’s estimated incubation window, not a claim that an entire community is at risk. WHO says people are not contagious before symptoms begin; spread is through direct contact with blood or other bodily fluids, or materials contaminated by them. That is why named-contact tracing, infection control in care settings and safe burial are central to containment. The Ministry also reported 267 samples tested across five laboratories by 6 October, with one positive; 4,971 health workers trained; and 652,584 travellers screened. These figures describe capacity and workload, not whether every contact has been reached. Updates on follow-up and test results will be more useful than screening totals alone. Bundibugyo is not the Ebola strain many people know This case involves Bundibugyo virus, a distinct Ebola-causing virus with no approved specific treatment or vaccine. Licensed Ebola vaccines and antibody treatments target Zaire ebolavirus, not this strain. Supportive care remains available: WHO says early intensive care, including fluid replacement and treatment of symptoms, can improve survival. WHO says evidence that Ervebo, a Zaire-strain vaccine, offers meaningful protection against Bundibugyo in people is insufficient. Its 1 September guidance recommends possible use only under research protocols. So “there is an Ebola vaccine” is not accurate shorthand for protection against this outbreak’s virus. Bundibugyo’s early symptoms can resemble malaria and other illnesses, making laboratory confirmation important. WHO gives a two-to-21-day incubation period; people become infectious after symptoms begin. Spread occurs through direct contact with bodily fluids or contaminated materials, and can be amplified by failures in health-care infection control or unsafe handling of bodies. This is why response hinges on triage, testing, follow-up and safe burial—not avoiding ordinary contact with every traveller. A regional outbreak, with a Kenyan test of preparedness Kenya’s Health Ministry links the case to a traveller returning from the DRC; his stop in Kampala does not make Uganda the source. WHO and Africa CDC declared Uganda’s Bundibugyo outbreak over on 27 August after 42 days without a confirmed case. The DRC outbreak remains active. WHO data through 3 October recorded 8,544 confirmed cases and 4,114 deaths there—figures not Kenyan cases and subject to revision. Kenya had prepared for importation. In September, WHO reported training for health workers and border stakeholders at Busia, Malaba and Lwakhakha, but also a staffing gap in night-time screening of small-scale traders at Busia. That was not this patient’s route; it shows why airport screening alone is not enough. Community alerts, after-hours coverage, laboratory turnaround and hospital infection control must connect. The confirmed case and death are serious, but one reported infection does not by itself show wider transmission in Kenya. The next indicators are whether the contacts and flight group are accounted for, anyone develops symptoms, and suspected cases are isolated and tested promptly. The Ministry directs the public to its official channels and toll-free line 719 for updates, and says people who are unwell should seek care at recognised facilities. Calm cooperation supports containment; stigma and speculation do not

Local SEO Leads Kenya (LSLK) 4.0(1) Nairobi Explore Build your reading streak0/3 today·Counts at 25% The ongoing Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has claimed more than 4,000 lives, making it the fastest-growing and second-deadliest on record. Health authorities confirmed 4,018 deaths among 8,300 confirmed cases across seven provinces. Efforts to contain the virus are increasingly hampered by protests over unpaid wages among frontline responders and violent resistance within affected communities. The Ministry of Health, Hygiene and Social Welfare released the updated figures on Friday, underscoring the severity of the 17th Ebola epidemic to strike the Central African nation. Since the outbreak was officially declared on May 15, 2026, it has outpaced the transmission rate of all previous crises. The overall case fatality rate currently stands at 48.4 percent, with 2,162 patients having formally recovered. The World Health Organization declared the crisis a Public Health Emergency of International Concern shortly after its onset. The rapid spread into new health zones, stretching from the epicentres in Ituri and North Kivu provinces to remote regions, continues to strain limited national and international health resources. The Bundibugyo Strain Challenge Unlike the recent outbreaks in the region, the 2026 epidemic is driven by the Bundibugyo ebolavirus. The pathogen presents a distinct challenge because existing medical countermeasures, including the widely deployed rVSV-ZEBOV vaccine and specific antiviral treatments, were developed exclusively for the Zaire ebolavirus. Currently, there is no approved vaccine or recognised antiviral treatment for the Bundibugyo strain. This medical limitation forces health agencies to rely heavily on traditional public health interventions: aggressive contact tracing, isolation, strict infection prevention protocols, and supportive clinical care. The pace of transmission has been unprecedented. The 2018–2020 Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo—previously the second-largest in history—took approximately 235 days to record 1,000 confirmed cases. The current epidemic surpassed the 1,000-case milestone within 40 days of response activation, fundamentally altering the baseline for epidemic forecasting in the region. Frontline Workers Demand Unpaid Wages The medical response has been severely disrupted by recurring administrative failures. In Bunia, the capital of northeastern Ituri province and the heart of the outbreak, health workers gathered this week to demand months of owed wages. Surveillance team members, who hold the critical responsibility of finding and monitoring people who came into contact with infected patients, joined the protests. Demonstrators waved placards reading "No money, no data" and "No payment for months" before being dispersed by local officials. The strikes have created dangerous blind spots in the epidemiological data, preventing authorities from mapping the exact transmission chains. The occupational hazards for those engaged in the response remain extraordinarily high. An aid worker with Médecins Sans Frontières contracted the virus while working in the country. The worker was evacuated on a special medical flight to the Netherlands late Thursday night and transferred to a high-level isolation unit at the Leiden University Medical Center. Comparison of the Largest Ebola Outbreaks in History Outbreak Period Primary Location Ebolavirus Strain Confirmed Cases Recorded Deaths 2014–2016 West Africa Zaire 28,600+ 11,300+ May 2026–Present Democratic Republic of the Congo Bundibugyo 8,300 4,018 2018–2020 Democratic Republic of the Congo Zaire 3,470 2,280 Violent Community Resistance Public health interventions are also battling intense local resistance. Widespread mistrust of government officials and health workers, compounded by chronic insecurity and historical grievances, has frequently erupted into violence against response teams. Earlier this week, Marie-Célestin Karondwa, a local politician with the ruling Union for Democracy and Social Progress party, was beaten to death by a mob at his home in Butembo, North Kivu. He had been publicly defending the government's outbreak containment measures. Following the fatal assault, his house was set on fire. The incident highlights the severe tensions between the state apparatus and communities who often view the Ebola response with deep suspicion, with some residents continuing to dismiss the virus as a manufactured hoax. Last month, authorities attempted to pivot to a "village-centred approach," aimed at empowering local leaders to manage surveillance and isolation protocols. However, the assassination in Butembo underscores the limits of this strategy when foundational trust is absent. International Funding and Data Gaps The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention indicated during its latest briefing that while the number of newly confirmed cases appears to be falling in certain hotspots, this trend must be interpreted with caution. The apparent decline is likely driven by escalating insecurity and the breakdown of community cooperation, which prevents surveillance teams from accurately recording new infections. International funding is slowly adapting to the scale of the emergency. The Canadian government recently announced $36 million to support the Ebola response in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and neighbouring Uganda. The funding is earmarked for public health operations, humanitarian assistance, and $4 million specifically directed toward the research and development of medical countermeasures for the Bundibugyo strain. Until targeted vaccines and therapeutics enter clinical trials, the trajectory of the outbreak remains entirely dependent on basic epidemiological control. With surveillance networks disrupted by strikes and violence, the true scale of the transmission network likely exceeds the official registry, leaving the timeline for containment entirely uncertain. Learn more Build your reading streak0/3 today·Counts at 25% Outbreak Surpasses Grim Milestone Across Multiple Provinces Authorities in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) have confirmed that the ongoing Ebola outbreak has now caused more than 4,000 deaths, marking a devastating escalation in one of the most severe public health crises the region has faced in recent years [[16]]. The outbreak, driven by the Bundibugyo virus strain, has spread far beyond its initial epicenter, with cases confirmed across at least seven provinces, including Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Haut-Uélé, Tshopo, Bas-Uélé, and Sud-Ubangi [[85]]. Health officials report that the total number of confirmed cases has surpassed 8,000, resulting in a case fatality rate of approximately 50 percent [[24]]. The rapid geographic expansion of the virus has overwhelmed local health infrastructure, forcing the Ministry of Health and international partners to stretch their resources across a vast and often inaccessible terrain. The Bundibugyo virus, while historically less widespread than the Zaire ebolavirus, poses a severe threat due to its high mortality rate and the logistical challenges associated with deploying targeted vaccines and therapeutics in active conflict zones. Community Mistrust and Security Challenges Containment efforts have been severely hampered by deep-seated community mistrust and ongoing insecurity, particularly in the eastern provinces of North Kivu and Ituri [[91]]. In these regions, armed conflict and the presence of numerous militant groups frequently disrupt contact tracing, safe burial practices, and vaccination campaigns. Health workers operating in these hotspots often face hostility from local populations who view the medical response with suspicion, a dynamic that has historically allowed the virus to spread undetected through remote communities. Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) and other frontline organizations have been forced to adapt their strategies, focusing on community engagement and decentralized care to bypass security roadblocks [[87]]. As part of the Ministry of Health-led response, MSF is currently conducting a major study following 20,000 frontline workers in Ituri and North Kivu to better understand the occupational hazards and transmission vectors within medical facilities [[87]]. Despite these efforts, the shortage of trained personnel and essential medical supplies remains a critical bottleneck, leaving many rural health centers ill-equipped to isolate suspected cases or manage severe hemorrhagic symptoms. International Response and Vaccine Limitations The World Health Organization (WHO) and the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) have mobilized emergency response teams to support the DRC government, but the scale of the outbreak continues to outpace the available resources [[24]]. Unlike previous outbreaks driven by the Zaire ebolavirus, which can be targeted with the highly effective rVSV-ZEBOV vaccine, the Bundibugyo strain requires different medical countermeasures that are currently in shorter supply. This biological distinction has complicated ring vaccination strategies, forcing health authorities to rely heavily on strict isolation protocols and intensive surveillance to break chains of transmission. The international community has been urged to increase financial and logistical support, as the outbreak threatens to destabilize an already fragile region. Neighboring countries, including Uganda, which has also experienced recent Ebola incidents, remain on high alert, implementing rigorous cross-border screening measures to prevent the virus from spreading internationally [[84]]. As the death toll climbs, the DRC's struggle to contain the Bundibugyo virus underscores the persistent vulnerability of conflict-affected regions to zoonotic diseases and the urgent need for more versatile, broadly effective vaccine platforms. Historical Context of DRC's Ebola Battles The Democratic Republic of Congo has a long and tragic history with the Ebola virus, having recorded its first outbreak in 1976 near the Ebola River [[93]]. This current crisis represents the country's 15th recorded epidemic, but it is distinguished by its unprecedented geographic reach and the involvement of the Bundibugyo species [[93]]. Historically, outbreaks in the DRC were confined to remote, heavily forested areas in the northwest, such as Equateur province, where containment was easier to manage due to lower population density and limited mobility [[93]]. The shift toward the densely populated and highly mobile eastern provinces has fundamentally altered the epidemiology of the disease. Urban centers and busy transit corridors in North Kivu and Ituri facilitate rapid transmission, making traditional quarantine measures far more difficult to enforce. Health experts note that the intersection of high population mobility, porous borders, and chronic underinvestment in rural healthcare has created a perfect storm for the virus, turning what might have been a localized event into a protracted national emergency. records.content: NanoViricides, Inc. (NYSE American: NNVC), a clinical-stage antiviral drug developer, has provided an update on its Phase II clinical trial of NV-387 Oral Gummies for the treatment of Bundibugyo Ebolavirus (BDBV) and other Ebola viruses in the Democratic Republic of Congo. The trial is proceeding as designed, with enrollment in Phase IIA beginning on or about Sept. 23, 2026. Phase IIA is intended to identify an optimal, well-tolerated dosing regimen and serve as a go/no-go step before Phase IIB, a randomized controlled trial designed to evaluate efficacy. The company said NV-387 is designed to attack the virus and reduce viral load and is delivered as an oral gummy that dissolves in the mouth without requiring water or swallowing effort. If successful, the oral treatment could be readily deployed in resource-limited settings, where traditional injectable Ebola therapies may be difficult to administer. NanoViricides characterized NV-387 as a broad-spectrum antiviral that mimics a host-side feature used by Ebola viruses and said there is a rationale for potential activity against Bundibugyo and other Ebola viruses. For full details, see the company’s press release . The news matters because the ongoing Bundibugyo outbreak in the DRC highlights the need for easy-to-use therapeutics that can be deployed rapidly in remote areas. An oral gummy that does not require refrigeration or trained personnel for administration could significantly improve outbreak response. NanoViricides, Inc. (NYSE American: NNVC) is a clinical-stage company creating special purpose nanomaterials for antiviral therapy. Its novel nanoviricideTM class of drug candidates is based on intellectual property and technology from TheraCour Pharma, Inc. Beyond Ebola, NV-387 is being developed as a broad-spectrum antiviral for RSV, COVID, Long COVID, Influenza, and other respiratory viral infections, as well as MPOX/Smallpox and Measles. The company’s other advanced candidate is NV-HHV-1 for Shingles. NanoViricides holds a worldwide exclusive perpetual license to TheraCour’s nanomedicine technology for several human viral diseases, including HIV/AIDS, Hepatitis B and C, Rabies, Herpes, Influenza, Dengue, and Ebola/Marburg viruses. The company’s progress with NV-387 could position it as a key player in pandemic preparedness and response. However, as is customary in drug development, the path to approval is lengthy and requires substantial capital, and there can be no assurance that any candidate will show sufficient effectiveness and safety for human clinical development. The latest updates relating to NNVC are available in the company’s newsroom at https://ibn.fm/NNVC . Photo: WHO/Ardo Farah #Ethiopia UN relief chief calls for safe, rapid access as teams work to deliver life-saving help The Under-Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs and Emergency Relief Coordinator, Tom Fletcher, said in a social media post that in northern Ethiopia, “our teams are working to get life-saving food, health and other help to people in need.” He called on all parties to give aid workers safe and rapid access. Meanwhile, ongoing hostilities continue to displace people across Central, North-Western and Eastern Tigray, although verified figures remain unavailable. The UN and its partners are prepared to resume aid operations in the northern regions, including Tigray, as and when they gain access. In the Amhara region, a Government-led effort to help people displaced by recent insecurity from the town of Kobo to their areas of origin was suspended following a deterioration in the security situation. The UN reiterates that any returns must be safe, voluntary, informed and dignified. #Ebola outbreak Democratic Republic of the Congo: UN, partners support scale-up of Ebola response The Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) says that the UN and its partners continue to support authorities in the Democratic Republic of the Congo in scaling up the response to the Ebola outbreak. As of 3 October, authorities had reported more than 8,500 confirmed cases and over 4,100 deaths. Transmission has accelerated in recent days, with 102 new confirmed cases reported on 3 October, compared with 66 the previous day. The provinces of Ituri and North Kivu accounted for more than 94 per cent of the new cases. North Kivu remains among the hardest hit. Contact tracing coverage stands at just under 68 per cent – well below the target of 95 per cent – complicating efforts to break chains of transmission. The UN and its partners are also concerned about movement restrictions introduced yesterday along several key roads in North Kivu as part of efforts to contain the Ebola outbreak. While intended to curb transmission, these measures could further constrain humanitarian access, the movement of aid workers, and the continuity of response operations in some locations. Meanwhile, in the provinces of Haut-Uélé and Ituri, OCHA continues to support the Government’s efforts to strengthen Ebola prevention and surveillance in high-risk mining communities. Kenya: first imported case of Ebola confirmed The Government of Kenya has confirmed the country’s first imported case of Ebola disease caused by the Bundibugyo virus. Kenyan authorities rapidly identified, isolated and tested the case, and response measures – including contact tracing, enhanced surveillance and public health monitoring – are already under way. The case underscores the regional risk, as transmission continues in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. The UN’s message is clear: the response must continue until transmission is stopped, alongside cross-border surveillance, regional coordination, preparedness and readiness. The World Health Organization and its partners are supporting Kenya’s Ministry of Health and National Public Health Institute in preparedness and response efforts. Isolation units across 27 high-risk counties have been identified, and Ebola surveillance tools have been updated so that suspected cases can be quickly identified, reported and investigated. The UN and its partners are supporting Government-led efforts to prevent further transmission, strengthen preparedness and response capacities, and ensure a coordinated regional response. The UN continues to encourage countries across the region to strengthen cross-border surveillance, screening at points of entry, contact tracing and coordination to detect and respond rapidly to cases. #Occupied Palestinian Territory Gaza: funding gaps, supply restrictions hamper water, sanitation support OCHA says that support for water and sanitation in Gaza is being held back by funding shortfalls and restrictions on the entry of critical supplies.* Items subject to import restrictions include engine oil, spare parts and equipment critical to keep vehicles and machines running. Partners say that shortages have caused a decline in water production at two desalination plants in southern Gaza, where equipment could not be properly maintained. This has resulted in a slight reduction in drinking water for roughly 500,000 people in Deir al Balah and Khan Younis. Across Gaza, partners estimate that three in every four families rely on water delivered by truck, until water infrastructure can be fully restored. Partners are delivering 25,000 cubic metres of drinking water every day through 3,200 collection points. However, the vehicles they use need maintenance – and access to certain areas is often suspended due to insecurity, particularly along the so-called “Yellow Line.” In the fourth week of September, partners distributed over 12,000 water containers with a 10-litre capacity each to help people collect water distributed by truck. Partners also provided thousands of trash cans, bags, sponges and dusters; 3,000 litres of dishwashing soap; 4,600 gloves and facemasks; nearly 1,300 litres of bleach; over 200 latrines; and hundreds of hygiene kits. Recently, shortages of import-restricted items have prevented the use of vehicles to collect and transfer solid waste, forcing reliance on donkey carts and UN trucks instead. In addition to approvals for restricted items, access must be restored to Gaza’s two landfills that are close to the Strip’s perimeter to prevent further accumulation of solid waste in populated areas. Sustained funding for fuel is also critical. West Bank: scores of Palestinians displaced after building demolished in East Jerusalem Humanitarian partners say that 69 Palestinians, over half of them children, were displaced in the West Bank today after Israeli authorities demolished their residential building in At Tur area of East Jerusalem. This is the highest number of people displaced in a single demolition in East Jerusalem since UN records began in 2009. The UN and its partners visited the area, and families there said that Israeli forces had prevented them from retrieving their belongings, which were left buried under the rubble. Partners assessed people’s immediate humanitarian needs and made sure they can receive rent support and essential items. So far this year, Israeli authorities have demolished or forced owners to demolish the homes of more than 1,800 Palestinians across the West Bank. Most were demolished for lacking Israeli-issued building permits, which are rarely granted to Palestinians in the affected areas. Humanitarian partners have provided them with emergency shelter, essential items and psychosocial support. *Donations made to UN Crisis Relief help UN agencies and humanitarian NGOs reach people in the Occupied Palestinian Territory with urgent support

Credit : Michel Lunanga/Getty NEED TO KNOW A Kenyan resident living in Congo flew to Nairobi, where he tested positive for Ebola Officials identified 55 contacts who will remain isolated for 21 days and receive testing The ongoing outbreak has sickened 8,442 people and is now the second largest Ebola outbreak on record Kenya officials have confirmed the first-ever case of Ebola in the country amid an ongoing outbreak of the rare Bundibugyo strain of the virus in the Democratic Republic of Congo. A Kenyan citizen residing in Congo had been ill for a month, and was treated in “several hospitals” in Congo, Kenya Health Minister Aden Duale said in an Oct. 6 press conference, per Reuters. The man traveled by road to Kampala, Uganda’s capital and, from there, flew on Oct. 3 to Nairobi, Kenya, on Jambojet Flight 8523, Duale said. Duale said that when the man arrived, he underwent the “normal public health screenings” but passed them. It’s the country’s first-ever case of Ebola, the BBC says. Ebola virus. Getty “We believe that the patient knew that he was already ill,” Health Ministry Director General Patrick Amoth said, saying that the treatment he had in Congo may have been “able to mask some of the symptoms,” which is why he passed the mandated health screening when he arrived at Nairobi International Airport. A relative took the patient from the airport directly to Nairobi Hospital, where he was admitted with fever, chills and bleeding beneath the skin. There, he tested positive for Ebola, Associated Press reports. The man was placed in isolation and given “supportive treatment”, but died on October 5. Officials have identified 28 people who were in contact with the man — including health care workers and family members — as well as 23 passengers who were on the flight, and four crew members. Amoth said the contacts will remain in isolation for 21 days, and after testing negative for the virus, they can be released. The disease is not considered to be airborne, and is not thought to be particularly contagious; however, it is infectious — meaning, it takes a small amount of contact with the virus to contract Ebola. The current outbreak of Ebola has sickened a confirmed 8,442 people, and killed 4,080, according to the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control. It’s now the second largest outbreak of Ebola on record, per the U.S. Centers for Disease Control, which adds that it “spreading substantially faster than previous Ebola outbreaks.” The patient died at Nairobi Hospital on Oct. 5. Credit: OutofAfrica / WPietsch / Alamy Stock Photo Subscribe to PEOPLE magazine to get the news, how-it-happened true crime stories and more — right to your mailbox. Ebola is caused by a collection of viruses called orthoebolaviruses. The Bundibugyo strain is a relatively rare strain of the virus, as NPR reports, and isn’t always included in standard testing for Ebola. This may have led to delays in identifying early Ebola cases in this outbreak. According to the CDC, someone infected with Ebola doesn’t spread the disease until they’re symptomatic. Symptoms can appear as late as 21 days after contact with an infected person, and begin with what are called “dry” symptoms of Ebola, like fever, joint and muscle pain, headaches and fatigue. The disease then progresses to the “wet” symptoms, which, along with vomiting and diarrhea, include bleeding from the eyes, mouth, nose and rectum. The virus spreads through contact with the bodily fluids of an infected person — alive or dead. But Johns Hopkins Medicine explains, it can also spread by touching items, like clothing or bedsheets, that have been in contact with body fluids. In response, the World Health Organization has outlined stringent guidelines for disinfecting and disposing of anything that’s been in contact with an infected person. Authorities said that the Kenyan man will be buried within 24 hours, according to the safety protocols. Health Cabinet Secretary Aden Duale announced the development, detailing the patient's complex travel route and the immediate containment measures activated at the country's points of entry. The deceased, a Kenyan citizen who had been residing in the DRC, travelled by road to Kampala, Uganda, before boarding a Jambojet commercial flight to Nairobi. The passenger arrived on Jambojet flight JM8523 from Entebbe on October 3 and subsequently tested positive for the virus at both the National Virology Reference Laboratory and the Kenya Medical Research Institute (KEMRI). The patient later succumbed to the disease, marking a critical moment for Kenya's epidemiological surveillance systems. Aggressive Contact Tracing and Isolation In response to the confirmed case, the Ministry of Health has launched an aggressive contact tracing operation to identify and monitor anyone who may have been exposed to the virus. Authorities have already identified and isolated twenty-eight primary contacts, including family members and the healthcare workers who attended to the patient upon arrival. These individuals are currently under strict medical surveillance and monitoring for any symptoms of the disease. Furthermore, health officials are actively pursuing an additional twenty-three passengers and four crew members who were aboard the same Jambojet flight. The airline has stated that it is working in close coordination with the Ministry of Health, Port Health Services, and other relevant aviation and public health authorities to trace these individuals and ensure they are placed under the necessary observation protocols. The rapid identification of these contacts is considered the most critical step in preventing any potential local transmission. Understanding the Bundibugyo Strain The Bundibugyo ebolavirus is one of the four species of Ebola virus known to cause severe disease in humans. While it is generally associated with a lower case fatality rate compared to the more notorious Zaire ebolavirus strain, it remains a highly dangerous pathogen that requires immediate and rigorous containment. The virus is primarily transmitted through direct contact with the blood, bodily fluids, or contaminated surfaces of an infected person who is showing symptoms. Public health experts emphasize that Ebola is not an airborne disease and is not spread by individuals who are infected but asymptomatic. This biological reality means that the risk to the general public remains low, provided that the identified contacts are properly managed and isolated. The Ministry of Health has reassured the public that the national health system is well-prepared, drawing on extensive experience from previous regional outbreaks and routine preparedness drills conducted at major entry points like Jomo Kenyatta International Airport. Because the patient transited through Uganda before entering Kenya, the case underscores the porous nature of regional borders and the necessity for seamless information sharing between neighboring states. Kenyan authorities are currently reviewing the thermal screening and health declaration forms utilized at the Entebbe and Nairobi airports to identify any potential gaps in the initial detection process. Jambojet, as the carrier involved, has faced intense scrutiny regarding its in-flight health protocols and the training of its cabin crew to recognize and manage medical emergencies involving infectious diseases. The airline's swift cooperation with health authorities is vital for ensuring that all potential exposure points within the aircraft are properly sanitized and that the manifest is accurately utilized for contact tracing. Aviation regulators are expected to issue updated advisories to all carriers operating within the East African Community. The Ministry of Health has urged citizens to remain calm but vigilant, advising the public to avoid contact with wild animals, practice rigorous hand hygiene, and immediately report any symptoms such as sudden fever, muscle pain, or unexplained bleeding to the nearest health facility. The latest figures were released by the health ministry on Thursday. They show that 4,018 people have died from among 8,300 confirmed cases in what has become the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history. More than 2,000 patients have recovered from the disease, the Reuters news agency notes. Congo announced an outbreak on May 15, caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus, which has no known treatment or vaccine. Medical workers work inside a mobile lab set up to test rapidly for the Ebola virus in Butembo, Congo, on Sept. 30, 2026. AP Photo / Sebastien Kitsa Musayi Some health workers gathered in Bunia, the capital of northeastern Ituri province, the heart of the outbreak, to demand payment for owed wages. They were quickly dispersed by officials. The protesting workers included surveillance team members, who identify people exposed to infected patients. They waved placards saying, "No money, no data!" and "No payment for months." Front-line workers have gone on several strikes since the start of the outbreak to demand payment, further hampering efforts to contain the disease. An aid worker with Médecins Sans Frontières, known in English as Doctors Without Borders, was infected with Ebola while working in Congo, the group said in a statement. The worker arrived late Thursday night after being flown to the Netherlands on a special medical flight and was transferred to a high-level isolation unit, the Leiden University Medical Center said in a statement. "The human cost of this crisis is unprecedented in the DRC, with communities facing the largest Ebola disease outbreak ever recorded in the country," MSF said. More than 50 health workers have died after contracting the virus. The World Health Organization has recently raised the alarm regarding the rapid geographical spread of the virus into new health zones, stretching limited resources. The Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said in its latest news conference that the number of confirmed cases is falling, but that could be attributed to insecurity and challenges in getting communities to cooperate in some of the hotspots. A Congolese politician was attacked and beaten to death earlier this week for defending government measures in dealing with the outbreak, highlighting tensions that have stretched both the health community and local resources. The attack on Marie-Célestin Karondwa, a local official with Congo's ruling Union for Democracy and Social Progress party, took place on Sunday at his home in Butembo, an Ebola hotspot in the eastern North Kivu province. His house was set on fire afterward and he died at a hospital of his injuries. Widespread mistrust of health workers and the authorities has hampered efforts to slow the Central African nation's 17th Ebola outbreak. Authorities last month launched a village-centered approach but those efforts are battling beliefs by some residents who dismiss Ebola as a hoax. There is also deep distrust in the country's government for reasons ranging from how it managed past Ebola outbreaks to chronic corruption.
